literal: Anicha flower, stalk without removing, she wore; for [her] waist, good will not sound drums.
translation: She wore the delicate Anicha flower without removing its stem; now, only ominous drums, and not auspicious ones, will sound for her fragile waist.
modern: அவள் அனிச்ச மலரின் காம்பைக் கிள்ளாமல் அப்படியே தலையில் சூடிக்கொண்டாள்; அதனால், அவளது மெல்லிய இடைக்கு நல்ல மங்கல ஒலிகள் ஒலிக்காது (இடை முறிந்துவிடும் என்பதால் சாவுப் பறையே ஒலிக்கும்).
explanation: This couplet uses playful exaggeration to praise the extreme delicacy of the heroine's waist. The Anicha flower is famous in classical Tamil poetry for being so delicate that it wilts when merely smelled. The heroine has worn this flower in her hair, but she neglected to remove its tiny stem (kāl). The poet humorously suggests that even this microscopic extra weight is too heavy for her incredibly slender waist (nugappu, a variant of nusuppu), causing it to be on the verge of breaking. Consequently, instead of joyful, auspicious drums (nalla paṟai), only the solemn drums of ruin will sound for her waist.
